sDescription: At age 75, English music manager Richard Cole passed away. His best-known role was serving as tour manager for Led Zeppelin spanning the years 1968 to 1980. Additionally, he wrote the book titled Stairway to Heaven: Led Zeppelin Uncensored.

Duran Duran expressed sadness and outrage after losing a High Court legal battle to recover United States rights for several of their most well-known tracks. The band contended that American copyright legislation permitted them to request a copyright reversion following 35 years. The contested songs included 'Girls on Film', 'Rio', and 'A View to a Kill'.

American saxophonist Bobby Keys passed away at his home in Franklin, Tennessee, due to cirrhosis. Beginning his touring career at age fifteen alongside Bobby Vee and fellow Texan Buddy Holly, Keys gained his greatest renown as the primary saxophonist for The Rolling Stones. According to legend, during a tour with the Stones, Keys filled a bathtub with Dom Perignon champagne and consumed the majority of it. His recording credits included albums by Harry Nilsson, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Delaney & Bonnie and Friends, George Harrison, John Lennon, Eric Clapton, Joe Cocker, and various other notable musicians.

Roger Taylor and Brian May opened the Queen Studio Experience - Montreux, an exhibition of Queen memorabilia at Mountain Studios in Switzerland, where they had recorded many classic tracks spanning seven albums and where Freddie Mercury recorded his last vocal. The exhibition would open to the public a day later.

Reggae singer Junior Murvin, best known for the 1976 hit song 'Police and Thieves', died in Jamaica aged 67. 'Police and Thieves' (produced by Lee "Scratch" Perry), was a hit in Jamaica and also took off in the UK where it found an audience with punk rock aficionados.

Led Zeppelin was honoured by Barack Obama for their major contribution to American culture and the arts. Wearing black suits and bow ties, Robert Plant, John Paul Jones, and Jimmy Page attended a White House dinner where they received Kennedy Centre Honours alongside other artists. During his tribute, Mr Obama remarked: "When Jimmy Page, Robert Plant, John Paul Jones and John Bonham burst onto the musical scene in the late 1960s, the world never saw it coming." The president also thanked the former group members for their good behaviour at the White House, referencing their past reputation for "hotel rooms being trashed and mayhem all around".

Scottish pianist, vocalist, lyricist, songwriter, producer, and co-creator of The Alan Parsons Project Eric Woolfson passed away from kidney cancer at the age of 64. Woolfson composed tracks for Marmalade, Frank Ifield, Dave Berry, Marianne Faithfull, The Tremeloes, and Peter Noone. Subsequent to the 10 successful albums created alongside Alan Parsons, his worldwide album sales surpassed 50 million.

At age 77, the American singer, actress, guitarist, songwriter, and civil and human rights activist Odetta passed away from heart disease. Her impact reached numerous prominent artists of the era's folk revival, such as Bob Dylan, Joan Baez, Mavis Staples, and Janis Joplin. Her track 'Take This Hammer' was selected by Time magazine for its 100 Greatest Popular Songs compilation. Additionally, Martin Luther King Jr. referred to her as the queen of American folk music.

Sharon and Ozzy Osbourne raised upwards of $800,000 (£389,032) for charity by auctioning belongings from their past residence in the US. Among the items purchased were a custom family pool table for $11,250 (£5,470), a set of Ozzy's signature round glasses for $5,250 (£2,553), a beaded wire replica of the Eiffel Tower from the kitchen for $10,000 (£4,862), and a pair of skull-decorated trainers worn by Ozzy that brought in $2,625 (£1,276).

David Mount, who played drums for Mud, passed away in London. The band achieved a 1974 UK No.1 single with 'Tiger Feet', which was the best-selling single of 1974, alongside 14 additional UK Top 40 singles.

For her role in the new musical 'Dreamgirls', which is based on the history of Diana Ross and The Supremes, 25 year old actress and singer Beyoncé was positioned to receive a £5m payment, making her set to earn a higher salary than any other Black actress for a film performance.

Dutch singer Mariska Veres from Shocking Blue died of cancer at the age of 59. Had the 1970 US No.1 & UK No.8 single 'Venus', (later covered by girl group of Bananarama). Shocking Blue was also responsible for the first Nirvana single, a cover of their song 'Love Buzz'.

Justin Hawkins, singer for the Darkness, spent two hours in detention at New York's JFK Airport when officers confused him with a fugitive sharing his appearance and name. Sue Whitehouse, who serves as Justin's manager and fiancee, secured his release by providing a tour itinerary demonstrating that he was in England on July 4th, the date of the offense.

Liam Gallagher, the vocalist for Oasis, faced arrest and assault charges following a physical altercation where he delivered a Kung-Fu kick to a police officer. Taking place at Munich's Bayerischer hotel, the confrontation resulted in the singer losing his front two teeth, alongside an unconscious Oasis security guard.
Singer Valerie Jones died aged 45. One-third of the sister group The Jones Girls, who sang back-up vocals with Lou Reed, Diana Ross, Aretha Franklin, Lou Rawls, Teddy Pendergrass and Betty Everett.

Thieves broke into the London home Madonna shared with Guy Ritchie. The raiders forced their way in through a basement door then took a set of car keys before loading up Guy Ritchie's car with some of the couple's possessions and driving off.

'One Sweet Day', a duet featuring Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men, claimed the No. 1 spot on the US singles chart. Following 'Fantasy', this achievement marked Carey as the first artist in history to secure two consecutive single debuts at No. 1.

MTV broadcast the complete 14-minute music video for Michael Jackson's Thriller for the initial time. Today considered the most influential pop music video ever made, it became the first music video inducted into the Library of Congress's National Film Registry in 2009 for its cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance.

American folk singer David Blue passed away at age 41 from a heart attack while jogging in Washington Square Park in New York. During the late 70s, he was a member of Bob Dylan's Rolling Thunder Revue. He composed the song 'Outlaw Man', which was recorded by the Eagles for their 1973 album Desperado.

An edit of the track "You Don’t Bring Me Flowers" by Barbra Streisand and Neil Diamond played a major role in reaching No. 1, originating at WAKY Radio in Louisville, Kentucky. WAKY Program Director Gary Guthrie created a spliced version combining the two solo tracks as a divorce "going-away gift" for his wife. Listeners connected with the emotional duet, leading WAKY to add it to regular rotation. Listener requests surged, and as news spread, stations across the country started broadcasting Guthrie’s edit. This widespread interest prompted Columbia Records to officially record the pair, bringing Diamond and Streisand together in the studio for the first time. The resulting studio recording reached the top of the charts in late 1978.

Rod Stewart held the top position on the UK singles chart with 'Da Ya Think I'm Sexy', marking his fifth chart-topper in the UK. A plagiarism suit filed by Jorge Ben Jor, a musician from Brazil, established that the track was adapted from his tune 'Taj Mahal'. In response, Stewart consented to give all royalties generated by the track to the United Nations Children's Fund.

Pink Floyd began photographing the cover for their upcoming album Animals at Battersea Power Station in London, England, positioning a massive inflatable pig between two of the station's towers. Although a marksman was hired to shoot the pig down if it broke loose, his services were unnecessary on the opening day. Because the marksman was not booked for the subsequent day, the inflatable drifted away after breaking its moorings, ultimately coming down in Kent. A local farmer retrieved it, reportedly angered that the object had ‘scared his cows.’

A maintenance worker from the building where Cindy Birdsong of The Supremes resided abducted her at knifepoint. She subsequently managed to get away without injury by leaping from his vehicle on the San Diego freeway. Four days later, authorities apprehended the abductor in Las Vegas.

The Monkees album, ‘Pisces, Aquarius, Capricorn and Jones Ltd’ went to No.1 on the US album chart. It was their fourth album to sell over a million copies, following ‘The Monkees’, ‘More Of The Monkees’ and ‘Headquarters’.

David Bowie put out 'Rubber Band' as his initial single for the Deram label. The track originated from a three-track audition tape utilized by Bowie's fresh manager, Kenneth Pitt, to secure his signing with the label. Even though music publications offered favorable reviews, the single underperformed commercially and failed to enter the UK charts.

The Beatles recorded a guest spot for the British television comedy show The Morecambe and Wise Show, performing the tracks 'This Boy', 'All My Loving', and I Want to Hold Your Hand, alongside taking part in comedy skits with Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise. The show aired on April 18, 1964.

US radio station KEX in Portland disc jockey Al Priddy lost his job following a broadcast of Elvis Presley's recording of 'White Christmas'. Station leadership explained that the track lacked the appropriate Christmas spirit.

Jarad Anthony Higgins was an American rapper, singer, and songwriter who performed under the professional name Juice Wrld. He rose to prominence through his 2018 diamond-certified single 'Lucid Dreams', which reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100. On December 8, 2019, Higgins passed away from a drug overdose.

American singer and songwriter Charlie Puth gained widespread recognition for co-writing and providing vocals on Wiz Khalifa's US No.1 single 'See You Again', which was featured on the Furious 7 soundtrack.

Tal Wilkenfeld is an Australian bass guitarist who has achieved global recognition through performances alongside prominent rock and jazz musicians such as Jeff Beck, Prince, Eric Clapton, Jackson Browne, Joe Walsh, and Mick Jagger.

American singer Britney Spears, known as the "Princess of Pop", has made a major cultural impact in the 21st century and is credited with helping revive the teen pop genre. She landed the 1999 US and UK No. 1 single 'Baby One More Time'—ranked among the best-selling singles in history—while her 1999 album Baby One More Time spent 82 weeks on the UK chart. Having sold over 150 million records globally, Spears ranks as one of the best-selling music artists in history, and Nielsen SoundScan placed her as the fourth best-selling female album artist of their era. Forbes named her the highest-paid female musician in the world twice, in 2001 and 2012. Spears has garnered numerous industry accolades, consisting of one Grammy Award, six MTV Video Music Awards, and seven Billboard Music Awards.

Canadian singer and songwriter Nelly Furtado released her debut album, Whoa, Nelly! (2000), which featured two top 10 hit singles, 'I'm Like a Bird' and 'Turn Off the Light'. Her third album, Loose (2006), emerged as her highest-selling album, achieving worldwide sales of 12 million copies.

Chris Wolstenholme is the bassist for the English rock band Muse, which achieved a UK No.1 album in 2003 with Absolution and a UK No.8 single that same year with 'Time Is Running Out'. Muse received five Grammy Award nominations and won Best Rock Album for The Resistance.
Donna Matthews is a Welsh musician who served as the lead guitarist for the Britpop band Elastica, which achieved the 1995 UK No.13 single 'Waking Up'.

Nate Mendel is an American bassist who has played with Foo Fighters, The Jealous Sound, Sunny Day Real Estate, and The Fire Theft. Additionally, Mendel was a member of Diddly Squat and the punk bands Christ On A Crutch.

English musician Rick Savage is best recognized as a founding member and bass guitarist of the rock band Def Leppard. The group achieved the 1987 UK No.6 single "Animal", while their 1987 worldwide No.1 album Hysteria stayed on the charts for more than two years and has accumulated worldwide sales of over 15 million copies. Recognized among the world's best-selling music artists, Def Leppard have achieved worldwide sales exceeding 100 million records.

Sydney Youngblood is an American-German singer, actor, and composer who scored several successful dance hits in the late 1980s and early 1990s, which includes the 1989 UK No.3 single 'If Only I Could'.

Jamaican musician Garth Dennis co-founded Black Uhuru and subsequently spent ten years as a member of The Wailing Souls. Growing up in Trenchtown, he formed friendships with Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, and Bunny Wailer. He passed away at the age of 72 on 9 December 2021 due to complications from pneumonia.

Ted Bluechel Jr served as a drummer and singer for the American Sunshine pop band The Association, known for their 1967 US No. 1 single 'Windy'. The band also performed as an opening act at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival.

Tom McGuinness, who played guitar and provided vocals, was a member of Manfred Mann, the group behind the 1964 UK and US No. 1 single 'Do Wah Diddy Diddy'. Later, as part of McGuinness Flint, he achieved the 1970 UK No. 2 single 'When I'm Dead And Gone'. McGuinness subsequently joined The Blues Band.

Ernest Warren was a singer with the Fifties doo-wop group The Spaniels. Their 1954 hit 'Goodnite, Sweetheart, Goodnite' appeared in films including American Graffiti and Three Men and a Baby. The Spaniels were among the initial artists to sign with Vee-Jay Records, which was the first large, independent, Afro-American-owned record label. Warren passed away on May 7, 2012.

Dr Peter Carl Goldmark created the long-playing microgroove record in 1945, an invention that subsequently transformed how audiences experienced music. On 7th December 1977, Goldmark died in an automobile accident.
